title: V838 Monocerotis revisited: Space phenomenon imitates art
caption: The light echo around the star V838 Monocerotis, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: IRAS 07015-0346, V838 Mon · constellation Monoceros · about 20000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, the Hubble Heritage Team (AURA/STScI) and ESA

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Swirling spirals of dust sweep across this Hubble image, lit by a red supergiant star at its middle. The star is V838 Monocerotis, and the glowing pattern is an expanding halo of light spreading into the interstellar dust around it. The pattern resembles Vincent van Gogh's 'Starry Night', with its bold whorls of light.

The illumination comes from a flashbulb-like pulse of light that the star gave off two years before the image was taken. As that light travels outward, it lights up successive parts of the surrounding dust, revealing spirals never seen before across trillions of kilometers of space. This effect is known as a light echo.

Van Gogh's sky came only from his imagination, but here nature produced something similar. V838 Mon lies about 20,000 light-years from Earth in the direction of Monoceros, which puts it on the outer edge of our galaxy.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.40 x 2.63 arcminutes) and distance (20000 light years), the frame spans roughly 14 × 15 light-years. Its light set out about 20,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The dust is visible only because it reflects the star's earlier outburst, and the faint halo would be far too dim to see without a large telescope.

explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took the image on February 8, 2004, and at the time it was the telescope's latest look at the star's expanding halo. Repeated views like this let astronomers follow the light as it moves outward through the dust.
alt: Swirling spirals of illuminated dust around a red star at the center.
